What if we told you there's a way to turn back the clock on your skin without going under the knife, without needles, and with virtually no downtime?

Welcome to the world of Focus Dual® by Lynton – the game-changing treatment that's giving our clients at Inga's Secrets Aesthetics the confidence boost they've been searching for.

𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗘𝘅𝗮𝗰𝘁𝗹𝘆 𝗶𝘀 𝗙𝗼𝗰𝘂𝘀 𝗗𝘂𝗮𝗹®?

Focus Dual® isn't just another beauty treatment – it's a medical-grade technology that combines two of the most advanced skin rejuvenation methods available today:

🔬 𝗛𝗜𝗙𝗨 (𝗛𝗶𝗴𝗵 𝗜𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗻𝘀𝗶𝘁𝘆 𝗙𝗼𝗰𝘂𝘀𝗲𝗱 𝗨𝗹𝘁𝗿𝗮𝘀𝗼𝘂𝗻𝗱) – Targets the deep structural layers of your skin, the same layers addressed in surgical facelifts

⚡ 𝗥𝗙 𝗠𝗶𝗰𝗿𝗼𝗻𝗲𝗲𝗱𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗴 – Works on the surface and mid-layers to improve texture, tone, and overall skin quality

Think of it as getting the benefits of multiple treatments in one powerful session.

𝗛𝗼𝘄 𝗗𝗼𝗲𝘀 𝗙𝗼𝗰𝘂𝘀 𝗗𝘂𝗮𝗹® 𝗔𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝗪𝗼𝗿𝗸?

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗛𝗜𝗙𝗨 𝗖𝗼𝗺𝗽𝗼𝗻𝗲𝗻𝘁: Imagine focused ultrasound energy as tiny, precise heat sources working deep beneath your skin's surface. This energy targets the SMAS layer (the same layer surgeons work with during facelifts) and creates controlled thermal zones that:

Stimulate your body's natural collagen production
Tighten existing collagen fibres
Lift and contour facial features naturally

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗥𝗙 𝗠𝗶𝗰𝗿𝗼𝗻𝗲𝗲𝗱𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗖𝗼𝗺𝗽𝗼𝗻𝗲𝗻𝘁: Ultra-fine needles create microscopic channels in your skin while radiofrequency energy heats the dermis. This dual action:

Improves skin texture and tone
Reduces fine lines and surface imperfections
Enhances overall skin quality and radiance

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗿𝗲𝘀𝘂𝗹𝘁? Your skin gets a complete rejuvenation from the deepest structural layers right up to the surface.

𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗖𝗮𝗻 𝗙𝗼𝗰𝘂𝘀 𝗗𝘂𝗮𝗹® 𝗧𝗿𝗲𝗮𝘁?

𝗙𝗮𝗰𝗶𝗮𝗹 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝗰𝗲𝗿𝗻𝘀:

Sagging jowls and loss of jawline definition
Double chin and neck laxity
Fine lines and wrinkles
Loose skin around the eyes
Overall facial volume loss
Uneven skin texture and tone

𝗕𝗼𝗱𝘆 𝗔𝗿𝗲𝗮𝘀:

Abdominal skin laxity (post-pregnancy or weight loss)
Loose skin on arms or thighs
Any area where you want tighter, firmer skin

𝗬𝗼𝘂'𝗿𝗲 𝗮𝗻 𝗶𝗱𝗲𝗮𝗹 𝗰𝗮𝗻𝗱𝗶𝗱𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝗶𝗳 𝘆𝗼𝘂:

Are experiencing early to moderate signs of ageing (typically 35-65+)
Want natural-looking results that develop over time
Prefer non-surgical alternatives to facelifts
Have busy lifestyles and can't afford lengthy recovery periods
Want to avoid repeated injectable treatments
Are looking for long-lasting results (12-18 months)

Have very severe skin laxity (surgical intervention may be more appropriate)
Are pregnant or breastfeeding
Have certain medical conditions (we'll discuss this during consultation)

𝗗𝘂𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗧𝗿𝗲𝗮𝘁𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁:

Sessions typically last 30-75 minutes depending on the area
Most clients describe the sensation as warm and tolerable
No anaesthesia required
You can return to normal activities immediately

Results continue improving for up to 6 months

𝟲 𝗺𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗵𝘀: Peak results achieved

✅ 𝗠𝗲𝗱𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗹-𝗴𝗿𝗮𝗱𝗲 𝘁𝗲𝗰𝗵𝗻𝗼𝗹𝗼𝗴𝘆 with proven safety records 

✅ 𝗢𝗻𝗴𝗼𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘀𝘂𝗽𝗽𝗼𝗿𝘁 throughout your skin transformation journey

She bought the dress. Tried it on. Then put on the same gray sweater she always wore.

The dress stayed on the bed.

Picture that room for a moment.

A hanger on the floor. One shoe by the door. A phone that keeps lighting up because her sister wants to know when she will leave.

Imagine a woman called Claire.

She is forty-one. She has a good life. People who love her. Work she is good at. A laugh that gets loud when she forgets to hold it in.

And a navy dress she has tried on three times.

She bought it for dinner. Nothing big. Just a night out with her sister, whom she had not seen in weeks.

In the shop, she loved the soft cloth. She loved the color. She held it up and thought, That is me.

At home, she did what she always did.

She tried one bra. Then a second. She pulled the front of the dress a little to one side. She stood straight. Then turned.

She was not trying to look like someone else.

She just wished she had more breast fullness to fill it the way she liked.

That was the wish. Small enough to wave away. Old enough to be tired of waving away.

Her phone lit up again.

She took the dress off.

When her sister came to get her, the gray sweater was on. The dress was still on the bed.

“I thought you got something new,” her sister said.

“I did.”

“Did it not fit?”

Claire looked at the bedroom door.

“It fits. I just don't like how I feel in it.”

Her sister did not rush to tell her she looked fine.

She sat on the edge of the bed.

“Do you want to tell me?”

It was such a small question.

Yet it gave Claire room to say the thing she kept making smaller.

“I want fuller breasts,” she said. “I have for years. And I feel silly saying that out loud.”

There. Said.

No tears. No great speech. Just a woman in a gray sweater, telling the truth beside a dress she liked.

Her sister nodded.

“Why silly?”

“Because there are bigger things to care about.”

“You care about those too.”

Claire laughed. A little.

She had spent years treating this wish like a guest who had stayed too long.

She would try to send it away. It would turn up again the next time she got dressed.

At a wedding. Before a trip. When she saw a top she loved and chose a different one before she even tried it on.

Most days, she did not think about it much.

That did not mean the wish was gone.

It meant she had built small habits around it.

Buy the higher neck. Keep the extra layer. Pick the outfit that takes less thought. Say the dress was not her style.

After a while, she forgot that those were choices.

They felt like rules.

Her sister picked up the hanger.

“You don't need my permission,” she said. “But you can look into it if you want.”

Claire had looked into it.

That was part of the trouble.

She had seen creams. Pills. Little pumps. Bold claims beside bright photos. Each new page seemed to say the last page had it wrong.

Then there was surgery.

She knew women who were happy with implants. She did not think they had made a bad choice.

She just did not want that choice for herself.

What she wanted felt plain.

From \u00a3199 for 24 hours of continuous recording.\n\nKey facts\n\n\t*  Price: \u00a3199 for 24 hours; \u00a3299 for 48 hours; \u00a3499 for 7 days\n\t*  What it records: a continuous ECG of every heartbeat for the whole wearing period, plus the times you note symptoms\n\t*  Detects: atrial fibrillation and other irregular rhythms, ectopic beats, fast rhythms such as SVT, slow rhythms and pauses, and whether your symptoms coincide with a rhythm change\n\t*  Does not detect: blocked coronary arteries, heart valve disease or heart failure; a Holter is a rhythm test, not a heart attack test\n\t*  How it works: posted to you free; fit it at home following the guide; wear it; return it in the prepaid bag; report emailed within 2 working days of receipt\n\t*  Report: analysed and written by a cardiologist; no GP referral needed\n\nYour questions answered\n\nCan I get a Holter monitor privately, without a GP referral?\n\nYes. Order online, choose 24 hours, 48 hours or 7 days, and the monitor is posted to you free with fitting instructions. You fit it yourself at home, wear it as you go about your normal life, and return it in the prepaid bag. A consultant cardiologist analyses the full recording and your report is emailed within 2 working days of the device arriving back. No referral, no hospital visit and no waiting list. On the NHS, a Holter is arranged through your GP and a cardiology department, typically with a wait of several weeks for the fitting and a further wait for the report.   How much does a Holter monitor test cost?\n\n\u00a3199 for a 24-hour recording, \u00a3299 for 48 hours and \u00a3499 for 7 days, including the device, free delivery both ways and the cardiologist's report. Private hospitals typically charge \u00a3250 to \u00a3450 for a 24-hour Holter plus a consultation fee of \u00a3200 to \u00a3300 to request and review it. You do not need to buy a monitor: the device is loaned for the recording period and returned.   What does a Holter monitor detect?\n\nAnything to do with heart rhythm. Atrial fibrillation, the commonest serious arrhythmia and a major cause of stroke, which often comes and goes and is missed on a single ECG. Ectopic beats, the skipped or thumping beats most palpitations turn out to be, and how many you have in a day. Fast rhythms such as supraventricular tachycardia. Slow rhythms, pauses and heart block, which cause dizziness and blackouts. And, most usefully, whether the symptoms you note in your diary happen at the same moment as a rhythm change, or whether your heart was beating normally when you felt them.   What can a Holter not tell me?\n\nWhether your coronary arteries are narrowed, whether you have had or are at risk of a heart attack, whether your valves or heart muscle are damaged, or what your blood pressure is doing. Those need different tests: a blood test for cardiovascular risk, an echocardiogram, a CT coronary angiogram or an exercise test. If you have chest pain on exertion, breathlessness lying flat or swollen ankles, see your GP rather than ordering a Holter. If you have chest pain now, call 999.   Should I choose 24 hours, 48 hours or 7 days?\n\nIt depends on how often you get symptoms. If they happen every day, 24 hours is usually enough to catch them. If they happen most days but not every day, 48 hours doubles your chance. If they happen a few times a week or less, choose 7 days: a 24-hour recording of a symptom that occurs weekly will most likely be normal and tell you nothing. For suspected atrial fibrillation that comes and goes, longer is better, because the diagnosis depends on catching an episode. If you are unsure, contact us before ordering.   How do I fit and wear the monitor?\n\nThe pack contains the recorder, electrodes and a step-by-step guide. Clean and dry the skin, attach the electrodes where the guide shows, connect the recorder and start it; it takes a few minutes. Then live normally: work, walk, exercise, sleep with it on. Keep a note of the time and what you felt whenever you have symptoms, because matching your diary to the recording is what makes the report useful. Keep the recorder dry; it must be removed for showers and baths and reattached afterwards.   Who analyses my recording, and what does the report contain?\n\nA consultant cardiologist reviews the entire recording, not a sample of it, and writes the report. It covers your average, minimum and maximum heart rate, any arrhythmias found and how long they lasted, the number of ectopic beats, any pauses or conduction problems, and what was happening on the ECG at the times you noted symptoms, with a clear conclusion. Take it to your GP if anything needs action; the report gives them what they need to refer you to cardiology if required.   What happens if the Holter finds something?\n\nThe report says what was found and how significant it is. Occasional ectopic beats in a structurally normal heart are common and usually need no treatment beyond reassurance. Atrial fibrillation needs a GP appointment promptly, because treatment to reduce stroke risk may be needed. Significant pauses, heart block or sustained fast rhythms need cardiology referral, which your GP can make with the report in hand. A normal recording during symptoms is also a result: it tells you your heart rhythm is not the cause and points the search elsewhere.   Is a Holter better than an Apple Watch or a home ECG device?\n\nFor diagnosis, yes. A smartwatch records a single lead for 30 seconds when you ask it to, which is useful for capturing a suspected atrial fibrillation episode you notice, and some flag irregular rhythms in the background. A Holter records continuously for the whole period, including while you sleep and during symptoms you cannot react to quickly, and the whole trace is read by a specialist rather than an algorithm. If a watch has flagged an irregular rhythm, a Holter is the natural next step to confirm it and quantify it.   What are the symptoms that warrant a Holter?\n\nPalpitations: a racing, pounding, fluttering or irregular heartbeat, or the sensation of skipped beats, particularly if they last minutes or come with breathlessness. Unexplained dizziness, light-headedness or fainting, especially without warning. Episodes of a very fast or very slow pulse you have noticed or a device has flagged. A history of atrial fibrillation you want to monitor. Or simply persistent worry about your heart rhythm that a normal resting ECG has not settled, because a ten-second ECG only shows what your heart was doing in those ten seconds.   How do I return the device, and how long until the report?\n\nPut the recorder and electrodes back in the original packaging and post it in the prepaid returns bag provided; no label or payment is needed. The recording is downloaded and verified when it arrives, analysed by the cardiologist, and the report is emailed to you within 2 working days of receipt, Monday to Friday excluding public holidays.   Can I use the Holter if I have a pacemaker, or for someone else?\n\nIf you have a pacemaker or implanted defibrillator, contact us before ordering: recordings can be analysed but need to be flagged. Same-day results if the laboratory receives your sample by 11am.\n\nKey facts\n\n\t*  Price: from \u00a3120 with your own sample collection; \u00a3165 at a Goodbody clinic; \u00a3185 with a nurse home visit\n\t*  From: 6 weeks of pregnancy, counted from the first day of your last period\n\t*  How it works: looks for Y-chromosome DNA from the baby in a venous blood sample from the mother: Y DNA found means a boy, none found means a girl\n\t*  Accuracy: 99.9 percent when the sample is taken from 6 weeks\n\t*  Results: the same day if your sample reaches the laboratory before 11am, Monday to Friday; otherwise within 1 to 2 working days\n\t*  Safety: a standard blood sample from your arm; no risk to you or your baby\n\nYour questions answered\n\nWhen can you find out the gender of your baby?\n\nWith a blood test, from 6 weeks of pregnancy. The baby's DNA is present in your bloodstream from early pregnancy, and from 6 weeks there is enough of it to test reliably for the Y chromosome. By comparison an ultrasound can usually see the sex from around 14 to 16 weeks, and the NHS anomaly scan at 18 to 21 weeks is when most parents in the UK find out. Non-invasive prenatal screening (NIPT) can also report sex from 10 weeks.   How early can you find out the gender of a baby?\n\n6 weeks is the earliest reliable point for a blood test. Before that, the amount of fetal DNA in your blood may be too low and a 'no Y detected' result could be wrong. Count from the first day of your last period, or use your dating scan if you have had one, and book the sample for 6 weeks or later. If you book earlier by mistake, we will help you rearrange the date.   How accurate is a gender blood test?\n\n99.9 percent when the sample is taken from 6 weeks of pregnancy and there is enough fetal DNA present. The test looks for the Y chromosome, which only males carry, so finding it is a definitive sign of a boy. A girl result relies on finding no Y DNA, which is why timing matters: too early and a boy's DNA may not yet be detectable. Taking the sample from 6 weeks avoids this. Twins and recent pregnancies can affect interpretation; see below.   Can you find out the gender at 8 or 12 weeks?\n\nYes, easily. The blood test works from 6 weeks onwards and becomes only more reliable as fetal DNA increases, so at 8 or 12 weeks the result is at its most dependable. At 12 weeks an ultrasound cannot usually tell reliably, so a blood test is the way to know at your 12-week scan rather than waiting until 20 weeks.   How does the gender blood test work?\n\nDuring pregnancy small amounts of the baby's DNA cross into your bloodstream. The laboratory extracts this cell-free DNA from a standard blood sample and looks for sequences from the Y chromosome. Because you have no Y chromosome yourself, any Y DNA in your blood must come from the baby, meaning a boy. If none is found, the baby is a girl. It is the same principle used in NHS-style non-invasive prenatal screening.   Is the test safe for my baby?\n\nYes. It is a standard blood sample taken from your arm by a trained phlebotomist or nurse, exactly like any other blood test. Nothing touches the baby, so there is no risk of miscarriage or harm, unlike the invasive procedures used decades ago to determine sex before birth.   How much does a gender blood test cost?\n\nFrom \u00a3120 at Goodbody Clinic when you arrange your own sample collection, \u00a3165 with the sample taken at one of our clinics, or \u00a3185 with a nurse home visit, including laboratory analysis and your result. Same-day results are available when the sample reaches the laboratory before 11am on a weekday. The NHS does not offer a gender test; it tells you at the 20-week scan if the sonographer can see, and only if you ask.   Can I do a gender blood test at home?\n\nThe sample needs to be a venous blood draw rather than a finger-prick, because the laboratory needs enough blood to extract fetal DNA and to avoid contamination from a partner's or son's DNA on the skin, which is a known cause of wrong results with mail-in finger-prick kits. You can have it done at home by booking a nurse visit, or choose your own collection and have a healthcare professional draw the sample.   When do I get my results?\n\nYour result is emailed the same day if your sample reaches the laboratory before 11am, Monday to Friday; otherwise within 1 to 2 working days. Clinic and nurse samples taken early in the week are the most likely to qualify. If you are planning a reveal, tell us and we will help you time the sample.   Can the test be wrong, and what about twins?\n\nWrong results are rare when the sample is taken from 6 weeks. The main causes are testing too early, so a boy's Y DNA is missed, and a vanishing twin or a very recent previous pregnancy, which can leave male DNA in the blood for a time. With twins, Y DNA found means at least one boy; no Y DNA means two girls, but the test cannot tell you both sexes if one is a boy. Tell us if you are expecting twins or have had a pregnancy in the last few months.   Does the test tell me anything else about my baby?\n\nNo. It reports only the baby's sex. It is not a screening test for chromosomal conditions such as Down's syndrome; that is the NIPT test, which is available from 10 weeks and reports sex as well. If you want screening for conditions as well as sex, ask about our NIPT options.   Is a gender blood test available on the NHS?\n\nNo. The NHS does not offer a blood test to find out the baby's sex, and NHS NIPT is only offered where screening shows a higher chance of a chromosomal condition. Most parents in the UK find out at the 18 to 21 week anomaly scan, if the position of the baby allows and the hospital's policy is to tell you. FSH and LH, made by the pituitary, drive the ovaries; oestradiol is the ovaries' response; the balance between them shows whether you are ovulating normally, approaching the menopause, or have a pattern such as PCOS. Prolactin, when raised, stops ovulation and periods. Testosterone, SHBG and the free androgen index show whether androgen levels are contributing to acne, excess hair or irregular cycles. Read together, with your cycle day and symptoms, they explain most hormonal causes of irregular periods and difficulty conceiving.   When is the best time to test for hormone imbalance?\n\nFor FSH, LH and oestradiol, days 2 to 5 of your cycle, counting the first day of full bleeding as day 1, because that is when the reference ranges apply and when a raised FSH is most telling. Prolactin, testosterone and SHBG can be tested at any time. If your periods are irregular, test whenever you can and tell us your last period date; if you have no periods, or use hormonal contraception, timing does not matter but the report will interpret accordingly. AMH, for ovarian reserve, can be added at a clinic appointment.   Can I test my hormone levels at home?\n\nYes. The finger-prick kit reports all seven markers, including oestradiol, from a few drops of blood, and gives the same result as a clinic sample when it is taken on the right day of your cycle and posted promptly. If you would rather not do the finger-prick yourself, book a five-minute venous draw at one of 250+ Goodbody clinics or a nurse home visit; the price and the report are the same apart from the collection fee.   Will the NHS do a hormone test?\n\nYour GP can test FSH, LH, prolactin and sometimes testosterone if you have irregular or absent periods, or after a year of trying to conceive (six months if you are over 36). Atrial fibrillation, the commonest serious arrhythmia and a major cause of stroke, which often comes and goes and is missed on a single ECG. Ectopic beats, the skipped or thumping beats most palpitations turn out to be, and how many you have in a day. Fast rhythms such as supraventricular tachycardia. Slow rhythms, pauses and heart block, which cause dizziness and blackouts. And, most usefully, whether the symptoms you note in your diary happen at the same moment as a rhythm change, or whether your heart was beating normally when you felt them.   What can a Holter not tell me?\n\nWhether your coronary arteries are narrowed, whether you have had or are at risk of a heart attack, whether your valves or heart muscle are damaged, or what your blood pressure is doing. Those need different tests: a blood test for cardiovascular risk, an echocardiogram, a CT coronary angiogram or an exercise test. If you have chest pain on exertion, breathlessness lying flat or swollen ankles, see your GP rather than ordering a Holter. If you have chest pain now, call 999.   Should I choose 24 hours, 48 hours or 7 days?\n\nIt depends on how often you get symptoms. If they happen every day, 24 hours is usually enough to catch them. If they happen most days but not every day, 48 hours doubles your chance. If they happen a few times a week or less, choose 7 days: a 24-hour recording of a symptom that occurs weekly will most likely be normal and tell you nothing. For suspected atrial fibrillation that comes and goes, longer is better, because the diagnosis depends on catching an episode. If you are unsure, contact us before ordering.   How do I fit and wear the monitor?\n\nThe pack contains the recorder, electrodes and a step-by-step guide. Clean and dry the skin, attach the electrodes where the guide shows, connect the recorder and start it; it takes a few minutes. Then live normally: work, walk, exercise, sleep with it on. Keep a note of the time and what you felt whenever you have symptoms, because matching your diary to the recording is what makes the report useful. Keep the recorder dry; it must be removed for showers and baths and reattached afterwards.   Who analyses my recording, and what does the report contain?\n\nA consultant cardiologist reviews the entire recording, not a sample of it, and writes the report. It covers your average, minimum and maximum heart rate, any arrhythmias found and how long they lasted, the number of ectopic beats, any pauses or conduction problems, and what was happening on the ECG at the times you noted symptoms, with a clear conclusion. Take it to your GP if anything needs action; the report gives them what they need to refer you to cardiology if required.   What happens if the Holter finds something?\n\nThe report says what was found and how significant it is. Occasional ectopic beats in a structurally normal heart are common and usually need no treatment beyond reassurance. Atrial fibrillation needs a GP appointment promptly, because treatment to reduce stroke risk may be needed. Significant pauses, heart block or sustained fast rhythms need cardiology referral, which your GP can make with the report in hand. A normal recording during symptoms is also a result: it tells you your heart rhythm is not the cause and points the search elsewhere.   Is a Holter better than an Apple Watch or a home ECG device?\n\nFor diagnosis, yes. A smartwatch records a single lead for 30 seconds when you ask it to, which is useful for capturing a suspected atrial fibrillation episode you notice, and some flag irregular rhythms in the background. A Holter records continuously for the whole period, including while you sleep and during symptoms you cannot react to quickly, and the whole trace is read by a specialist rather than an algorithm. If a watch has flagged an irregular rhythm, a Holter is the natural next step to confirm it and quantify it.   What are the symptoms that warrant a Holter?\n\nPalpitations: a racing, pounding, fluttering or irregular heartbeat, or the sensation of skipped beats, particularly if they last minutes or come with breathlessness. Unexplained dizziness, light-headedness or fainting, especially without warning. Episodes of a very fast or very slow pulse you have noticed or a device has flagged. A history of atrial fibrillation you want to monitor. Or simply persistent worry about your heart rhythm that a normal resting ECG has not settled, because a ten-second ECG only shows what your heart was doing in those ten seconds.   How do I return the device, and how long until the report?\n\nPut the recorder and electrodes back in the original packaging and post it in the prepaid returns bag provided; no label or payment is needed.
